claims.text: Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi increases the stacking-fault energy of the resulting FeNiCrMn alloy.
Higher stacking-fault energy shifts dynamic deformation from twinning toward dislocation cross-slip and recovery.
The shift toward cross-slip-mediated recovery preserves a favorable strength–ductility balance across varying temperatures and strain rates.
The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy begins in a solidified, homogeneous solid-solution state.
Dynamic mechanical testing over controlled temperatures and strain rates, coupled with high-resolution characterization, can test the proposed mechanism.
Slip, cross-slip, and twinning are active and competitive at low to intermediate temperatures and strain rates in the proposed regime.
Stacking-fault-energy variation alters the balance between deformation twinning and cross-slip-mediated recovery.
The Co-free alloy will exhibit more cross-slip events than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi under identical dynamic conditions.
The Co-free alloy will exhibit less deformation twinning than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi under identical dynamic conditions.
The macroscopic strength–ductility balance of the Co-free alloy will remain comparable to that of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi within the stated regime.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi typically exhibits more deformation twinning under similar dynamic loading conditions.
At very high temperatures or extremely high strain rates, alternative deformation or phase-transformation mechanisms may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Processing history may affect the stacking-fault-energy difference and the relative activation of cross-slip and twinning.
Failure to observe a statistically significant cross-slip increase and corresponding twinning decrease in the Co-free alloy would falsify the proposed mechanistic shift.
A significant deviation of the Co-free alloy's strength–ductility balance from the baseline would falsify the predicted macroscopic outcome.
